tip: принесите (prinesite = bring) uses the -ите ending, the polite or plural command form you use with strangers.
за собой (za saboy = behind oneself) uses the reflexive pronoun себя (sebya), which points back to the subject of the command.
через (cherez = in) plus accusative gives time from now: через десять минут (cherez desyat minut = in ten minutes).
несёт (nesyot = is carrying) is from нести (nesti), used for carrying something in hand while on foot in one direction.
предложили (predlazhili = offered) is 3rd-person plural with no subject, meaning she was offered: ей (yey = to her) is dative.
вёл (vyol = was leading) is from вести (vesti), used for leading a person or animal on foot: вёл коня (vyol kanya = led a horse).
радоваться (radavatsya) takes the dative, so the thing you are glad about is погоде (pagode = weather): радуемся погоде (raduemsya pagode).
Russian doubles the negative: никому (nikamu = to no one) still needs не (ne) before говори (gavari = tell).
The instrumental marks what you wash with: холодной водой (khalodnay vadoy = with cold water), no preposition needed.
The word for 'this' changes by gender: этот (etat) for masculine nouns like товар (tavar = product), эта (eta) for feminine, это (eto) for neuter.
нравится (nravitsya) puts the liker in the dative: ей нравится (yey nravitsya = to her it pleases). The liked thing is the subject.
интересуюсь (interesuyus') takes the instrumental for the topic, with no preposition: историей (istoriey = in history).
улыбается (ulybayetsya) takes the dative for who you smile at: детям (detyam = at the children). Russian smiles 'to' someone.
отказывается (atkazyvayetsya) uses от plus the genitive for what is refused: от помощи (ot pomashchi = help).
чувствую себя (chuvstvuyu sebya): the reflexive себя is required to say how you feel: чувствую себя хорошо (...harasho = I feel good).
обращается (abrashchayetsya) takes к plus the dative for turning to someone: к врачу (k vrachu = to a doctor).
извиняюсь (izvinyayus') uses за plus the accusative for what you apologize for: за опоздание (za apazdaniye = for being late).
хотел бы (khatel by) softens want into 'would like', gentler than хочет (khochet = wants). бы plus past makes a polite wish.
бы plus a past-tense verb makes the conditional 'would': он бы написал (on by napisal = he would write). бы can shift position in the clause.
сердится (serditsya) uses на plus the accusative for who you are angry at: на брата (na brata = at her brother).
дороже (darozhe = more expensive) is the comparative; what you compare against takes the genitive with no word for 'than': того (tavo = that one).
везёт (vezyot) is impersonal 'to be lucky'; the lucky person goes in the dative: мне везёт (mne vezyot = I am lucky), with no 'I' subject.
сейчас (seychas) means 'now', but with a future verb it means 'in a moment': сейчас вернусь (seychas vernus' = I will be right back).
умываюсь (umyvayus') ends in the reflexive -сь (-s', from -ся) meaning wash oneself, so no separate 'my face' is needed: я умываюсь (ya umyvayus').
за plus the instrumental marks a static location: за деревом (za derevam = behind a tree). Motion to behind would take the accusative.
With чем (chem = than) the comparison is spelled out and needs a comma: свежее, чем вчера (svezheye, chem vchera = fresher than yesterday).
самый (samyy) plus an adjective forms the superlative 'the most': самый дорогой (samyy daragoy = the most expensive).
The liker goes in the dative with нравиться (nravitsya = to like): им (im = to them) means 'they like'. What is liked is the true subject.
заниматься (zanimatsya) takes the instrumental, not the accusative: занимался музыкой (zanimalsya muzykay = studied music), never музыку (muzyku).
её зовут Анна (yeyo zavut = literally 'they call her') is how Russian says 'her name is', with no verb 'to be named'.
